title: Penalties & Ref Signals
description: The flags you'll actually see on a broadcast, what the ref's arms are doing, and why.

entries.explanation: A blocker grabs and hangs onto a defender — jersey, arm, or a bear hug — instead of just pushing him. Blockers can use their hands, but they can't grab and restrict.
entries.signal: The ref grabs one wrist with the other hand and pulls it down in front of his chest, like he's caught himself by the arm.
entries.whenCalled: Constantly — it's the most common flag on big runs and long pass plays, and it wipes them out. When a huge gain comes back for no reason you can see, it's usually holding.
entries.example: A 40-yard run comes back because a guard tackled the defensive end who was about to make the stop.

entries.explanation: An offensive player flinches, jumps, or moves after getting set but before the snap. The play is blown dead immediately — the offense doesn't get to run it.
entries.signal: Both forearms rotate over each other in front of the chest, a rolling "revving up" motion.
entries.whenCalled: Most often in loud road stadiums when linemen can't hear the snap count, and on obvious passing downs when they're jumpy about the pass rush.
entries.example: 3rd and 8 in a deafening stadium — the left tackle flinches early and now it's 3rd and 13.

entries.explanation: A defender is on the wrong side of the ball when it's snapped — or jumps across and touches someone before it. The mirror image of a false start, but on the defense.
entries.signal: Hands on hips, like a disappointed parent.
entries.whenCalled: When pass rushers try to time the snap and guess wrong, or when a hard count by the quarterback baits them into jumping. Offenses will take a free deep shot when they see a defender jump.
entries.example: The QB's fake snap count draws the defensive end across the line — free play, so he launches one deep.

entries.term: Pass Interference (spot foul in college, 15-yard max)
entries.explanation: A defender grabs, shoves, or tangles up a receiver while the ball is in the air, before it arrives. Defenders can play the ball — they just can't play the man to stop the catch.
entries.signal: Both arms pushed forward from the shoulders with open hands, a shoving motion.
entries.whenCalled: On deep balls where the beaten defender panics and grabs. One of the most argued calls in football because contact happens on almost every pass.
entries.example: The receiver is a step behind the corner on a deep ball, so the corner hooks his arm before it lands — flag, big gain awarded.

entries.explanation: Forcible contact to an opponent's head or neck, or leading with the crown of the helmet, especially against a defenseless player. College football's most serious safety rule: it's always reviewed, and if confirmed the player is ejected.
entries.signal: The ref gives the personal-foul signal — one wrist striking down on the other above the head — and after review, signals the ejection.
entries.whenCalled: On big hits to receivers stretched out mid-catch or sliding quarterbacks. The stadium holds its breath during the review because a star player's game (and possibly the next half) is on the line.
entries.example: A safety launches helmet-first at a receiver's chin — reviewed, confirmed, and he's done for the day.

entries.explanation: A hit that goes beyond playing football: shoving someone out of bounds after the whistle, piling on a downed runner, or a late hit on the quarterback after the throw.
entries.signal: The personal-foul signal — one wrist striking down on the other above the head.
entries.whenCalled: After the play is effectively over — the ball carrier is already out of bounds or on the ground. Often the flag that turns a defensive stop into a fresh set of downs.
entries.example: The defense forces a punt, but a late shove after the whistle gives the offense 15 yards and a new drive instead.

entries.explanation: The play clock hits zero before the offense snaps the ball. Pure clock management failure — nobody touched anybody.
entries.signal: Arms folded across the chest, one over the other.
entries.whenCalled: Coming out of confusion — a slow huddle, a late play call, or the QB trying to change the play and running out of time. Also taken on purpose sometimes to give the punter more room.
entries.example: The sideline can't get the call in, the QB is screaming at the line, and the :00 flashes — five yards backward.
